dependent-manual-operation: An operation solely by means of directly applied manual energy, such that the speed and force of the operation are dependent upon the action of the operator ([[iec-56]] 3.104.9, IEV 441-16-13). The closing or opening of the [[circuit-breaker]] is carried out directly by the hand of the operator, with no stored or auxiliary energy interposed; consequently the making speed cannot be guaranteed. For this reason [[iec-56]] explicitly excludes from its scope any circuit-breaker fitted with a closing mechanism for dependent manual operation, because a rated short-circuit making current cannot be specified and such operation may be objectionable on safety grounds (scope, [[iec-56]] clause 1). Contrast with [[independent-manual-operation]], where stored energy de-couples the result from operator effort, and with [[stored-energy-operation]].
stored-energy-operation: An operation by means of energy stored in the mechanism itself prior to the switching operation and sufficient to complete the specified operating cycle under predetermined conditions ([[iec-56]] 3.104.11, IEV 441-16-15). The energy (commonly a charged spring, or compressed gas or hydraulic fluid in the [[operating-mechanism]]) is accumulated in advance, then released on command so the closing or opening speed is independent of the operator. This guarantees a defined making speed, allowing a rated short-circuit making current to be assigned to the [[circuit-breaker]]. It underlies fast auto-reclosing duty, and contrasts with [[dependent-manual-operation]], where speed depends on the operator. Compare [[independent-manual-operation]], a stored-energy variant in which a manual action charges and then releases the store.
independent-manual-operation: A stored-energy operation in which the energy originates from manual power, stored and released in one continuous operation, such that the speed and force of the operation are independent of the action of the operator ([[iec-56]] 3.104.12, IEV 441-16-16). The operator's hand movement (typically charging a spring) accumulates the energy, which is then released by a mechanism so that the closing speed of the [[circuit-breaker]] is fixed and cannot be slowed by hesitation. It is a special case of [[stored-energy-operation]] using human rather than auxiliary power, and is distinguished from [[dependent-manual-operation]], where the result depends directly on the operator's effort. The charging and release functions reside in the [[operating-mechanism]].
instantaneous-release: A release which operates without any intentional time delay ([[iec-56]] 3.104.17, IEV 441-16-32). Once its initiating quantity reaches the set value, the release acts at once to trip the [[operating-mechanism]] and open the [[circuit-breaker]], the only delay being the inherent response time of the mechanism. The term qualifies the time characteristic rather than the actuating quantity, so an [[over-current-release]] without intentional delay is an instantaneous over-current release. It contrasts with the [[definite-time-delay-over-current-release]] and inverse time-delay types, which deliberately postpone tripping. A [[making-current-release]] behaves instantaneously during a closing operation.
making-current-release: A release which permits a [[circuit-breaker]] to open, without any intentional time delay, during a closing operation, if the making current exceeds a predetermined value, and which is rendered inoperative when the circuit-breaker is in the closed position ([[iec-56]] 3.104.18). It guards the closing stroke: should the breaker be closed onto a fault, the high making current trips the [[operating-mechanism]] at once so the contacts re-open. Because it is disabled once the breaker reaches the closed position, it does not duplicate the protective function of an [[over-current-release]] during normal service. Its time characteristic is effectively that of an [[instantaneous-release]], and it complements the trip-free behaviour required of the mechanism.
over-current-release: A release which causes a [[circuit-breaker]] to open, with or without time delay, when the current in the release exceeds a predetermined value ([[iec-56]] 3.104.19, IEV 441-16-33). It senses the main-circuit current (directly or via a transformer) and, on reaching the operating current and current setting (3.104.27, 3.104.28), actuates the [[operating-mechanism]] to trip the breaker, providing overload and short-circuit protection. The release may be an [[instantaneous-release]] or incorporate a time delay, giving the [[definite-time-delay-over-current-release]] and inverse time-delay over-current release variants; by construction it is either a direct or an indirect over-current release. Related current-sensing types include the [[reverse-current-release]] (d.c. only) and the [[making-current-release]].
definite-time-delay-over-current-release: An [[over-current-release]] which operates after a definite interval of time which is independent of the value of the over-current ([[iec-56]] 3.104.20, IEV 441-16-34). On the current in the release exceeding its predetermined setting, a fixed, pre-set time delay elapses before the release actuates the [[operating-mechanism]] to open the [[circuit-breaker]]; raising the fault current does not shorten that interval (unlike an inverse time-delay over-current release, where operating time falls as current rises). The defined delay supports time-graded discrimination between series protective devices. It contrasts with the [[instantaneous-release]], which has no intentional delay. The opening time is measured with any such integral time-delay device set to its minimum ([[iec-56]] 3.105.32).
reverse-current-release: A release, applicable to d.c. only, which causes a [[circuit-breaker]] to open when the current passes in the reverse direction and exceeds a predetermined value ([[iec-56]] 3.104.26, IEV 441-16-43). It senses the direction as well as the magnitude of current, and on a sufficiently large reversal it actuates the [[operating-mechanism]] to trip the breaker, protecting sources such as batteries or rectifiers against back-feeding. It is one of the current-operated releases alongside the [[over-current-release]] and may act with or without intentional delay, the no-delay case being an [[instantaneous-release]]. Being a d.c. phenomenon, it sits apart from the a.c. duties that are the main subject of [[iec-56]].
interlocking-device: A device which makes the operation of an item of equipment dependent upon the position or operation of one or more other pieces of equipment ([[iec-56]] 3.104.31, IEV 441-16-49). Fitted to the [[circuit-breaker]] or its [[operating-mechanism]], it permits or prevents a closing or opening operation according to defined conditions, for example blocking closure unless an associated disconnector or earthing switch is in the correct position, thereby enforcing a safe operating sequence and protecting personnel and plant. It is functionally related to the anti-pumping device (3.104.30) and to the circuit-breaker with lock-out preventing closing (3.104.32), both of which similarly constrain operation of the mechanism.
operating-mechanism: The assembly that stores and delivers the energy needed to close and open the [[circuit-breaker]] and that carries the releases and interlocks acting on the contacts. In [[iec-56]] it is treated under "operating devices," which fall within the standard's scope together with their auxiliary equipment (scope, [[iec-56]] clause 1); the complete breaker including its operating devices must be capable of completing the rated operating sequence (3.102). According to its energy source the mechanism realises [[stored-energy-operation]], [[independent-manual-operation]] or [[dependent-manual-operation]] (the last excluded from scope). It houses the trip-free linkage and is acted upon by the [[over-current-release]], [[making-current-release]], [[instantaneous-release]] and the [[interlocking-device]]; recharging time of the operating mechanism is a tested characteristic.
